Self-Conscious Emotions in Sport and Exercise: Relationships of Implicit and Explicit Processes of Authentic and Hubristic Pride and Physical Activity


Sascha Leisterer-Härtig and Enno Winkler

Department of Sport Science, Leipzig University

Author Note

Sascha Leisterer-Härtig http://orcid.org/0000-0002-0493-8464

Enno Winkler http://orcid.org/0009-0008-0665-3447

Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Sascha Leisterer-Härtig, Department of Sport Science, Leipzig University, Jahnallee 59, Leipzig, Saxony, Germany, Email: sascha.leisterer@uni-leipzig.de

Abstract

Self-conscious emotions play a crucial role in sports and exercise by reflecting self-related goal achievements. Traditionally, these emotions are explained through explicit attributional processes. However, implicit processes that influence self-related goal orientation are often overlooked.

Self-Conscious Emotions in Sport and Exercise: Relationships of Implicit and Explicit Processes of Authentic and Hubristic Pride and Physical Activity

Hypotheses

Hypothesis 1: The implicit achievement motive correlates positively with authentic pride. In contrast, hubristic pride is associated with social dominance, reflecting the power motive, which leads to our second hypothesis: Hypothesis 2: The implicit power motive correlates positively with hubristic pride. As authentic pride relates to pro-social behavior and hubristic pride is associated with more anti-social behavior, our third hypothesis is: Hypothesis 3 is: The implicit affiliation motive correlates positively with authentic pride and negatively with hubristic pride. Additionally, in our fourth hypothesis, we assume that implicit motive component cues highlight situations as favorable for either authentic or hubristic pride: Hypothesis 4: Hope for success, hope for control, and hope for social belonging correlate positively with authentic pride; fear of failure, fear of loss of control, and fear of social rejection correlate positively with hubristic pride. Second, we hypothesize that causal attribution styles, as explicit regulation processes, correlate with either authentic or hubristic pride. This leads to the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 5: Individuals who tend to attribute their achievements, power, or social gains internally, variably, controllably, and specifically will report higher levels of authentic pride. Hypothesis 6: Individuals who tend to attribute their achievements, power, or social gains internally, stably, uncontrollably, and globally will report higher levels of hubristic pride. Third, based on existing literature, we hypothesize that authentic and hubristic pride are associated with physical activity parameters. This leads to the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 7: Authentic pride and its associated regulation processes correlate with higher physical activity parameters. Hypothesis 8: Hubristic pride and its associated regulation processes correlate with lower physical activity parameters.

H1: Positive correlation between achievement motive and pride H2: Positive correlation between power motive and hubris H3: Positive correlation between affiliation motive and pride, negative correlation between affiliation and hubris H4: Positive correlation between hope and pride, Positive correlation between fear and hubris H5: Positive correlation between internal, variable, controllable, specific attribution and pride H6: Positive correlation between internal, stable, uncontrollable, global attribution and hubris H7: Positive correlation between PA parameters and pride H8: Negative correlation between PA parameters and hubris

Study 1

Participants

Participants were adults with specific goals (e.g., running a marathon, competing in a triathlon, aesthetics, bodybuilding) and/or pre-defined workout routines (e.g., running routine, weight training routine). A sample size calculation performed before data collection using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) for testing one-tailed point biserial correlation with |ρ| = .5, α = .05, and 1 – β = .95 indicated a necessary sample size of N = 34. As an incentive, participants were offered feedback on their results and suggestions for improving their workout routine motivation. N = 41 participants completed the survey. Participants who reported not following a workout routine were excluded. The resulting final sample consisted of N = 32 recreational athletes who had a mean age of 34.69 years (SD = 13.7; range = 19–64), including 19 females, 8 males, 2 participants who identified as diverse, and Three who did not report their gender. Participants followed individual workout routines averaging 6.79 hours per week (SD = 4.04; range = 2–15) with a self-rated intensity (perceived exertion on a 1-10 scale) of 5.41 (SD = 1.74). Sports included running (n = 10), triathlon (n = 6), weight training (n = 5), and other endurance sports (n = 11). Missing values amounted to 15% of all data.

Analysis

First, implicit motives for achievement, affiliation, and power motives were z-standardized. The gender-balanced T-scores for the motive components according to >>>>>>> MC Clelland’S scoring procedure?? <<<<<<<<. were calculated. The entire data was checked for normal distribution. Applying the Shapiro-Wilk test, the weekly training distance (W = 0.724; p < .001), weekly training duration (W = 0.896; p = 0.008) and perceived exhaustion (W = 0.905; p = 0.013) as well as fear of rejection (W = 0.929; p = 0.042) were not normally distributed. Second, descriptive statistics were calculated. Third, due to the small sample size and normality violations, Spearman rank correlations were calculated. For the analysis, Version 4.5.0 of the programming language R (R Core Team, 2024) was used.

Results

Descriptive Statistics

Table 1 presents descriptive statistics, including mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis. The sample represents medium authentic pride and medium positive affect, low hubristic pride and low negative affect. Additionally, the sample shows a slightly stronger implicit affiliation motive but regular motive components in all 3 implicit motives. Further, the sample intended to report more internal, variable, and less uncontrollable attribution styles. Figure 2 visualizes the distribution of these variables.

Hypothesis testing

Exploratory analyses revealed significant correlations between pride and positive affect (Ρ = 0.48, p = .006); pride and fear of rejection (Ρ = -0.46, p = .009); hubris and negative affect (Ρ = 0.52, p = .002); weekly training duration and training distance (Ρ = 0.58, p = .002). The implicit affiliation motive (Ρ = 0.43, p = .023) and dynamic attributions (Ρ = 0.38, p = .046) correlated with training duration. Negative affect correlated with fear of failure (Ρ = 0.67, p < .001), fear of rejection (Ρ = 0.58, p = .001), locus (Ρ = -0.42, p = .017) and controllability (Ρ = 0.42, p = .017). The achievement motive correlated with the implicit affiliation (Ρ = 0.48, p = .009) and power motives (Ρ = 0.47, p = .009). Furthermore, fear of failure correlated with fear of rejection (Ρ = 0.52, p = .007), and fear of loss of control (Ρ = 0.51, p = .008). Finally, uncontrollable and internal attributions showed a correalation (Ρ = -0.79, p < .001).

Study 2

Analysis

We excluded participants manually if they reported data on less than two training sessions, if they did not participate in a structured training programme, or if they were neither runners nor triathletes. Subsequent analyses were performed using the R language (R Core Team, 2024). 17% of all values were missings. Since the questionnaires were sent out in weekly intervals, we expected autocorrelation between measurement points. We visually assessed the autocorrelation structure between measurement points: The variograms for all models indicated that autoregressive noise might be present: The semivariance changed substantially with distance between observations. Thus, we included an autocorrelation structure of order 1 (AR1), and compared the model quality with and without a correlation matrix.

Time was not included as predictor, since we did not expect a trend over time. To disentangle within and between-person-effects (see Wang and Maxwell (2015)), the time-varying predictors (pride and positive affect) were cluster-mean-centered, and the stable predictors (attribution style and implicit motives) were grand-mean-centered.
Lastly, we z-standardized all predictors for easier interpretation.

The results for the hierarchical linear models are presented separately for each the dependent variables of this study: session distance, session duration and rate of perceived exhaustion. We used interaction terms of pride with positive affect, causal attribution and implicit motives to predict these dependent variables. The predictors were added in three steps: First, the interaction term of pride and positive affect, second, the interaction terms of pride and attribution styles, and third, interaction terms of pride and implicit motives. We then decided on the appropriate model based on fit indices (AIC, BIC, log-likelihood, marginal/conditional R²) and explanatory power, and then examined the model quality, checking for normal distribution of residuals by inspection of Q-Q plots and Shapiro-Wilk-tests, homoscedasticity by examination of residual plots, absence of multicollinearity by calculation of the variance inflation factor, and linearity and distribution of outliers by visual inspection.Linearity was assessed by plotting each predictor against the outcome variable and examining LOESS-smoothed lines. On the individual level 2, we assessed normality of residuals and homoscedasticity.

Results

Session distance

In these models, we used interaction terms of pride with positive affect, causal attribution and implicit motives to predict running distance. The running distance was z-standardized within sessions speeds below five km/h, between five and 20 km/h and over 20km/h. We added predictors to the null model in three steps: First, the interaction term of pride and positive affect, second, the interaction terms of pride and attribution styles, and third, interaction terms of pride and implicit motives. The result is shown in Table 3.

The intraclass correlation coefficient was ICC = 0.25. Regarding autocorrelation between the measurements, the autoregressive parameter was φ = -0.71, 95% CI [-0.8854548, -0.3681785], indicating a tendency that higher values were followed by lower values of session distance, and vice versa. Model 3 included significant predictors and the lowest log-likelihood, it also fit significantly better than the same model without a correlation matrix (χ² = 11.59, df = 18; p < .001). Thus, Model 3 was selected for further analysis of statistical assumptions and the discussion.

The residuals were normally distributed (p = .095 ). Figure 3 shows a QQ-plot and scatterplot of the residuals. Here, the residuals are skewed to the left, indicating a slight deviation from the assumption of homoscedasticity.

The variance inflation factor ranged from vifmin = 1.38 to vifmax = 4.61.

Figure 4 shows substantial deviations from linearity. Figure 5 shows the distribution of outliers in the residuals by each individual.

The marginal and conditional R-squared values, representing the portion of variance explained by the fixed effects and the random effects respectively, were R2marginal = 0.25 and R2conditional = 0.663.

On the individual level (level 2), the residuals were not normally distributed (p = .017). No deviation from the assumption of homoscedasticity was present (p = .252).

Several interaction terms emerged as significant predictors: The interactions between pride and positive affect (b = 0.39, p = .015), and achievement motive (b = 0.58, p < .001) were positive, meaning that the effect of pride on the training distance in the next session is stronger when there is a high achievement motive or a high positive affect (in the previous session). The interaction terms between pride and globality (b = 0.393, p = .015), the affiliation motive (b = -0.72, p = < .001) and the power motive (b = -0.81, p < .001) were negative: When globality, affiliation or power are high, pride reduces the running distance in the next session.

Session duration

The parameters for this model that predicted session duration are shown in Table 4. The ICC was ICC = 0.48.

None of the models identified significant predictors of session duration. With an autoregressive coefficient of φ = -0.39, 95% CI [-0.39, 0.32], modelling autocorrelation did not improve the model fit significantly (p = .817). The model with the correlation matrix (Model 3) was retained for further examination.

The Shapiro-Wilk-test indicated a deviation from normality (p < .001). A slight deviation from the normal distribution of residuals and the assumption of homoscedasticity is apparent in Figure 6.

The variance inflation factor ranged from vifmin = 1.08 to vifmax = 3.4.

Figure 8 shows the predictors plotted against session duration to assess linearity.

Figure 7 shows two outliers in the residuals of the model.

The marginal and conditional R-squared values were R2marginal = 0.12 and R2conditional = 0.68.

On the individual level (level 2), the Shapiro-Wilk-test suggests non-normality (p = .009). No deviation from the assumption of homoscedasticity was present (p = .637).

Session Rate of Perceived Exhaustion

The regression coefficients are shown in Table 5. The third model with all predictors shows the lowest AIC and log likelihood. With φ = -0.42, 95% CI [-0.42, 0.35], a correlation matrix resulted in a worse fit ( p 0.84), so we used the model without the correlation structure, since it showed the lowest AIC and log likelihood and was tested for statistical assumptions and model quality.

A more stable attribution style predicted a lower RPE, and so did the interaction terms of pride with positive affect, pride with a more external locus of control, pride with a higher implicit affiliation as well as a higher power motive. Only the interaction between pride and the implicit achievement motive predicted a higher rate of perceived exhaustion for each session.

The residuals show a deviation from the assumption of normality, as indicated by a Shapiro-Wilk-test (p = .011). Figure 9 shows the deviation from the normal distribution in a QQ-Plot along with the distribution of residuals. The linear patterns that emerge in the residuals are a result of the discrete values in the session RPE data.

The variance inflation factor ranged between vifmin = 1.09 and vifmax = 2.72.

The marginal and conditional R-squared values, representing the portion of variance explained by the fixed effects and the random effects respectively, were R2marginal = 0.32 and R2conditional = 0.53.

Figure 10 shows the predictors plotted against the target variable.

On the individual level (level 2), the residuals were not normally distributed (p = .017). No deviation from the assumption of homoscedasticity was present (p = .252).

Several interaction terms emerged as significant predictors: When a person had a tendency to more stable attributions, session RPE was reduced (b = -0.462, p = .021). Pride predicted the session rate of perceived exhaustion negatively if positive affect in the last session was high (b = -0.183, p = .009), if people had a more external attribution style (b = -0.317, p = .003), and if the affiliation motive (b = -0.521, p = = .013) or power motive (b = -0.352, p = .048) were high. If the achievement motive was high, higher pride also predicted a higher RPE (b = 0.406, p = .007).

Discussion

The variance inflation factors suggest low multicollinearity (for a discussion see O’brien, 2007).
